redress

/rih-DRESS/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Redress means to set right a wrong or injustice — to correct it and make up for the harm that someone has suffered.

The tribunal was created to redress the losses of families whose land had been seized without payment.

Example

When a records check revealed that a scoring error had wrongly failed dozens of nursing students over a decade, the university moved to redress the wrong: it corrected every transcript, refunded the affected semesters, and paid for the licensing exams the graduates had been forced to retake.

The university did more than admit the mistake — it set the injustice right and made up for the harm each student had suffered, and that combination of correcting a wrong and repairing its damage is exactly what redress means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

remedy: To remedy is to fix a problem or put a bad situation right — you remedy a leak, a shortage, or a mistake, and no one need be at fault. Redress is narrower and heavier: it sets right a wrong done to someone, and it implies making up for the harm suffered.

recompense: To recompense is to repay someone for a loss or an effort, often with money and often with no admission that anything unjust occurred. Redress goes further: it treats the loss as a wrong, and it aims to set the whole injustice right rather than merely to write a check.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

entrench: to fix a wrong so firmly in place that it becomes ever harder to undo

Where it sits · how much of the wrong the response takes back

acknowledge → redress → undo

acknowledge vs. redress: Acknowledge is weaker than redress: acknowledging a wrong only admits that it happened, while redressing it goes further and actually sets it right.

undo vs. redress: Undo is stronger than redress: a redressed wrong has been repaired and paid for, but an undone wrong is erased entirely, as though it had never happened at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: again, back

Root — dress: from Old French drecier, 'to straighten, set upright, arrange,' from Latin directus, 'straight'

Put it together: Redress comes from Old French redrecier, 'to set straight again, to stand back upright' — re- ('again, back') plus drecier ('to straighten,' from Latin directus, 'straight'). To redress a wrong is literally to straighten what was bent out of true, which is why writers speak of redressing past injustices: old wrongs being set back upright.

Use the root in a new word: address: Rather than let the tenants' noise complaints pile up unanswered, the building manager chose to address them at the next meeting, one by one.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal — law, policy, and history writing

Redress takes the wrong itself as its object: you redress an injustice, an imbalance, or the harm done to someone — never the offender, who is punished instead. A mere technical fault or error is remedied or corrected, not redressed, because no one has been wronged. The word is common in participle form — a commission charged with redressing historical wrongs — and it doubles as a noun: families who lost their land went to court to seek redress.
